title: Frigaliment Importing Co. v. B.N.S. International Sales Corp.
summary: The buyer failed to prove that “chicken” in these contracts meant only young broilers rather than also including stewing hens.
notes: The transaction predates the CISG. Its international parties do not make the historical court’s analysis a CISG holding. The notes compare trade usage with the rules for interpreting writings and ask which party should bear uncertainty about unfamiliar terminology.

sections.Parties: Frigaliment, a Swiss buyer, sued B.N.S., the New York seller of frozen poultry, for breach of the contractual description of the goods. Judge Friendly decided the dispute in the federal district court under the New York sales law applicable to the transaction.
sections.Material Facts:
Two contracts made in May 1957 called for United States fresh-frozen chicken, Grade A, government inspected, eviscerated, and packed in specified weight ranges. The smaller birds weighed about one and one-half to two pounds; the larger birds weighed two and one-half to three pounds. The larger birds cost 33 cents per pound. When the first shipment arrived, the buyer discovered that the larger birds were mature stewing hens rather than young broilers suitable for frying. It promptly protested. A second shipment was sent and then stopped at Rotterdam.

The parties had negotiated partly through an intermediary and partly in German-language cables that nevertheless used the English word “chicken.” The buyer argued that this deliberate word choice excluded the broader German word for chicken. The intermediary’s account of the negotiations pointed the other way: the seller had asked what kind of chicken was wanted and understood the response to permit any kind satisfying the description. The seller was new to the poultry trade. Market evidence also showed that young broilers of the larger size cost more than the contract’s 33-cent price.
sections.Procedural History: The buyer brought a warranty action alleging that the birds did not correspond to the description in the contracts. After considering the parties’ communications, testimony, regulatory terminology, prices, and conduct, the district court dismissed the complaint with costs. The opinion supplies the court’s findings and conclusions.
sections.Issue: Did the contractual word “chicken,” read in the parties’ commercial context, exclude stewing hens, and did the buyer prove the narrower meaning on which its claim depended?
sections.Holding: No. The buyer bore the burden of establishing its narrow interpretation and did not carry it. The decision determines the meaning of these contracts; it does not supply a universal definition of chicken.
sections.Reasoning:
A dictionary offered both a broad meaning and the buyer’s narrower meaning, so ordinary usage did not decide the dispute. Nor did the smaller weight category control the larger one: the fact that small birds necessarily would be young did not establish that all birds had to be young. Testimony about the industry was conflicting, and some witnesses used additional words such as “broiler” in their own transactions. That weakened the claim that the unqualified word necessarily carried the buyer’s meaning.

The government classifications referenced in the description treated several kinds of birds as chickens. The price was also significant: the seller’s broad interpretation was commercially plausible, whereas the narrow interpretation would have required it to supply the larger young birds at a loss. The court tested the seller’s claimed understanding against objective evidence rather than simply accepting an undisclosed intention. The buyer’s prompt objection showed consistency in its position, but did not establish that the seller had agreed to that position. The different kinds of evidence had to be considered together, with the burden of proof resolving the remaining uncertainty.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: This case shows how an apparently simple word can require a factual inquiry into negotiations, specialized usage, incorporated standards, and price. It connects the formation-stage question of objective assent to interpretation of an agreement both sides acknowledge.

topics.assent: The parties’ different understandings are tested against the meaning objectively supported by their communications and context.
topics.interpretation: The court weighs competing meanings of the contractual description rather than looking only at a dictionary.
topics.trade-usage: Conflicting trade evidence and the seller’s newcomer status prevent an automatic inference of the buyer’s specialized meaning.
topics.governing-law: The historical international sale is analyzed under the domestic sales law applicable to that transaction.
